# Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (Game Boy Advance)

## Development and Release

The Game Boy Advance (GBA) version of *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* stands as a landmark achievement in portable gaming, representing one of the earliest successful translations of a sixth-generation console sports title to a handheld device . Developed by Vicarious Visions and published by Activision, the game was conceived and executed with remarkable speed and technical ingenuity, overcoming significant hardware limitations that had previously discouraged such ambitious ports [), ]. The project officially commenced in August 2000, following an initial handshake agreement with Activision made at E3 in May 2000 . The development team began preliminary research and development work using early GBA dev kits as early as April 2000, but the official start date for the project is cited as either April 6, 2001, or August 2000, with the project concluding in April 2001 after less than a year of full-scale development [), ]. This rapid turnaround was crucial for securing its position as a launch title for the GBA in North America and Europe , .

The central challenge faced by Vicarious Visions was the severe constraints of the GBA hardware, which included limited cartridge space, no native support for real-time 3D polygonal rendering, and a restrictive audio system , . To address the lack of storage capacity, the team could not use the sprite-based animation frames required by other versions, which would have exceeded the available cartridge space . Instead, they engineered a custom C++-based 3D engine capable of real-time rendering of polygonal skater models, which were composed of over 300 polygons each [), ]. For the environments, a different approach was necessary; instead of attempting complex real-time rendering, the levels were built using pre-rendered 2D backdrops combined with the 3D-skater model to create a convincing illusion of depth , . This technique was complemented by software masking to handle character occlusion when skaters passed behind objects, ensuring visibility [), ]. Level geometry itself was defined mathematically rather than stored as bitmaps, further conserving precious memory space . The physics calculations, another critical component, were performed in 3D using heavily optimized assembly code, including clever workarounds for the GBA's lack of a hardware division function .

A pivotal design decision was the adoption of a fixed isometric viewpoint, a departure from the behind-the-back third-person perspective of the original PlayStation version , . This choice was not a compromise but a deliberate adaptation to the GBA's capabilities . The isometric view, described as a "3/4 overhead perspective" or a "fixed diagonal camera view," allowed for smooth scrolling and provided depth cues through shadows, creating a "3D-like" effect , , . While some reviewers noted the initial disorientation caused by this perspective—where pressing right could turn the skater left depending on their orientation—it was ultimately deemed a functional necessity that enabled the game's ambitious visual presentation on the handheld screen . The audio implementation also presented hurdles; the GBA lacked the Red Book audio streaming capability of the PlayStation CD-ROM, making it impossible to include the full-length licensed soundtrack . As a result, the music was truncated into shorter instrumental versions, a necessary trade-off for portability . The soundtrack was entirely original, composed by Manfred Linzner, and implemented using Shin'en Multimedia's advanced GAX sound engine to maximize the quality of the two dedicated PCM channels [), ), ].

The game's status as a launch title was integral to its identity and marketing. It was released in North America on June 11, 2001, and in Europe on June 22, 2001, positioned alongside the debut of the Game Boy Advance console itself [), , ]. In Japan, the game was published by Success under the title 'SK8: Tony Hawk no Pro Skater 2' and launched later on December 14, 2001 , . This strategic placement ensured high visibility and cemented its reputation as a flagship title for the new platform. The development team, led by Project Manager Jesse 'Agent' Booth and Executive Producers Karthik Bala and Tobi Saulnier, successfully demonstrated that complex console experiences could be faithfully recreated on a handheld, setting a new standard for what was possible in portable gaming , . The game was praised for being "extremely faithful" to the console versions, even going so far as to reuse Neversoft's PlayStation source code for physics and tricks, adapting it to run on the GBA via a proof-of-concept validated by Nintendo , . This fidelity extended to the inclusion of all 13 playable professional skaters from the original, including Tony Hawk himself, and the meticulous recreation of seven levels, five from *THPS2* and two from the first game, plus one secret unlockable level [, /Walkthrough), ].

## Gameplay and Features

The gameplay of *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* on the Game Boy Advance is a testament to Vicarious Visions's ability to translate the complex mechanics of a sixth-generation console experience onto a handheld platform . At its core, the game faithfully replicates the spirit of the original, emphasizing progression from street skating to park skating, and rewarding players with massive combo chains and high scores , . The control scheme was meticulously adapted for the GBA's compact form factor, using the D-pad for movement and grinding balance, the A button for initiating grinds, the B button for jumping and crouching, and the shoulder buttons for executing tricks , . Specifically, the L Button toggles between Nollie and Ollie flips, while the R Button is used for grabbing tricks and switching grind styles . This layout was designed to feel intuitive for veterans of the series, though some players reported finger fatigue during extended sessions involving complex trick combinations . The game's trick system includes the fundamentals of skateboarding: ollies, grinds, wall rides, and aerial spins, allowing for the construction of lengthy combos that rack up points [, )]. A unique feature enabled via Mode-7 emulation is a "trick zoom" function, which provides a closer look at trick execution .

The game offers three primary modes of play, mirroring the structure of the console versions [)]. Career Mode is the main goal-driven experience, where players select one of thirteen skaters and progress through a tour of various locations, completing time-limited goals to earn cash and medals [, )]. These objectives include collecting S-K-A-T-E letters, hidden video tapes, money, and breaking specific objects, as well as performing location-specific tricks [), /Walkthrough)]. Winning competitions, which take place in Marseille, France, and Ventura, California, requires earning a medal (Gold, Silver, or Bronze) in the final session to advance [/Walkthrough)]. Free Skate mode offers unlimited time to explore the levels and practice tricks without pressure, while Single Session mode presents a two-minute high-score challenge [), ]. Within Career Mode, players can spend earned money to upgrade their skater's stats, such as Air, Hangtime, Speed, Spin, and Rail Balance, as well as purchase signature tricks . Each skater starts with three locked signature moves and has three customizable slots for additional special tricks .

The game's level design is a highlight, featuring seven distinct courses that are nearly identical in layout to their PlayStation counterparts , . These include four regular levels—Hangar (Meacham Field, Texas), School II (Southern California), Warehouse (Troy, New York), and New York City—and two competition levels, along with one secret unlockable level [/Walkthrough)]. Each level contains a checklist of objectives that must be completed to earn the highest score, including collecting scattered items like pilot wings or hall passes, locating hidden video tapes, and hitting all the rails and gaps on the course [), /Walkthrough)]. The scoring system is based on combo length and trick difficulty, with diminishing returns applied to consecutive tricks and significant multipliers awarded for spinning the board multiple times (e.g., a 900° spin is worth six times the base value) . Landing tricks cleanly adds a Perfect modifier for a bonus, while sloppy landings reduce the score . Despite its faithfulness, the GBA version makes several notable omissions due to hardware and time constraints. The Track Editor and Create-a-Skater modes, present in the console releases, were cut to conserve cartridge space [), ]. Additionally, a two-player multiplayer mode was omitted because of the compressed development schedule [), ]. The developers also deliberately removed non-skating elements common in real-world skating, such as police encounters, helmets, and street punks, streamlining the experience to focus purely on action and progression , .

## Reception and Sales

Upon its release, *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance received widespread acclaim from both critics and consumers, establishing itself as one of the most impressive and highly-rated games of 2001 . Its positive reception was driven by its remarkable technical achievement, faithful recreation of the console experience, and strong gameplay loop, all packaged within a polished launch title for the new GBA platform , . The game garnered a Metacritic score of 95 out of 100 and a GameRankings score of 89.88%, placing it among the top-rated titles of its generation . These scores were notably higher than those of many other major 2001 releases, including contemporaries like *Halo: Combat Evolved*, *Grand Theft Auto III*, and *Final Fantasy X*, underscoring its exceptional quality in the eyes of reviewers . IGN, a prominent gaming publication, awarded the game its prestigious "EDITORS' CHOICE" distinction, describing it as a "hand-held gem" lauded for its "cool graphics," "killer soundtrack," and "epic gameplay" , . The guide praised its extensive roster of 13 playable skaters and its streamlined focus on pure skateboarding action , .

Reviewers consistently highlighted the game's impressive visuals, which were considered "outstanding" and "unbelievable" for a handheld device . The use of real-time 3D polygonal models for the skaters, rendered without textures that were visually imperceptible at the small screen size, was a standout feature , . The fluidity of the animations and the detailed, recognizable level layouts were frequently commended , . One review gave the graphics and gameplay a perfect 10/10 rating, declaring it the "ultimate GBA game for launch" with no discernible flaws . The control scheme was also rated highly, receiving a 10/10 for being optimized for portable use, despite acknowledging potential for finger fatigue during long sessions , . The audio was similarly praised for its high-quality rock, hip hop, and skate punk music, as well as authentic sound effects, with a recommendation to use headphones for the best experience , . Even critiques tended to be minor; one reviewer noted that the music was only "half decent" but still not bad, and while the crash effects were realistic, the characters never sustained injuries beyond a "death" state . Another critic pointed out the disorienting nature of the isometric camera but concluded that it worked "very well" overall , .

The positive critical consensus was mirrored by strong user reception. On GameSpot, a sample of 23 visible reviewers showed broad approval, with 19 giving scores of 7 or higher . The median user score was around 8, indicating a generally favorable opinion among early players . The game's success was not limited to critical praise; it was also a significant commercial hit. By August 2006, it had sold 680,000 copies in the United States, generating $24 million in revenue . This performance placed it at the 38th highest-selling Game Boy Advance, Nintendo DS, or PlayStation Portable game in the U.S. during the specified period, demonstrating its enduring popularity . The game's commercial success was further bolstered by a strong showing in Japan, where *Famitsu* magazine awarded it a score of 33 out of 40, indicating a very positive reception in its home market . The combination of critical acclaim and robust sales solidified the GBA version's legacy as a flagship title that proved the viability of complex, graphically ambitious games on a portable platform, setting a high bar for future releases , .

## Legacy and Impact

The legacy of *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance extends far beyond its immediate commercial and critical success. It is widely regarded as a pioneering piece of development history that fundamentally altered perceptions of what was possible on a handheld gaming device . The game broke down industry assumptions that complex, polygonal, third-person sports games were too resource-intensive to be successfully ported to consoles like the GBA . Vicarious Visions's innovative solutions to the platform's hardware limitations—such as their custom real-time 3D engine, the clever use of isometric perspective to simulate depth, and the mathematical definition of level geometry—became a benchmark for the entire industry [, ), ]. The technical prowess displayed in the GBA version was so influential that it became a reference point for other developers. Digital Eclipse, for instance, explicitly cited the *THPS2* engine as a source of inspiration—and shared "awkwardness"—when developing their own isometric engine for *Spyro the Dragon: Season of Ice* on the same platform . Similarly, the engine was reused by Vicarious Visions for their own subsequent GBA title, *Jet Set Radio*, and its technical achievements influenced peer studios, cementing its status as a de facto standard for spatial navigation on the GBA circa 2001–2002 , .

In the context of the *Tony Hawk* franchise, the GBA version served as a crucial bridge, bringing the popular series to a new audience on the burgeoning handheld market [)]. It established a precedent for faithful yet reimagined adaptations, proving that the core appeal of the games could be preserved even when translated to a different medium with vastly different constraints . The success of this port paved the way for more entries in the series on the GBA, including *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3* (released March 4, 2002) and *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4* (October 23, 2002), both published by Activision [), ]. By demonstrating the viability of the franchise on portable hardware, it helped ensure the continued relevance of the *Tony Hawk* brand in the era of handheld gaming. The game is often contrasted favorably with earlier, less faithful adaptations of the series on the Game Boy Color, with critics describing it as "a more faithful version" and a "rather solid" entry in the handheld lineup .

Ultimately, *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance is remembered as a defining moment for the platform. It was not merely a competent port but a creative reinterpretation that respected the source material while embracing the unique possibilities and constraints of the GBA . Its success proved that developers could achieve remarkable graphical and mechanical fidelity on the handheld, inspiring a wave of more ambitious titles in the years that followed. The game's legacy is one of innovation and influence, serving as a case study in how technical ingenuity and a deep understanding of a platform's capabilities could lead to the creation of a "hand-held gem" that remains celebrated decades after its release , . It remains a benchmark against which all other GBA ports are measured, a testament to the vision of Vicarious Visions and the enduring appeal of the *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater* series .

Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (GBA) established a precedent for faithful yet reimagined adaptations, proving that the core appeal of the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater series could be preserved even when translated to a different medium with vastly different constraints.

The success of the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (GBA) port paved the way for more entries in the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater series on the Game Boy Advance, including *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3* (released March 4, 2002) and *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4* (October 23, 2002), both published by Activision.

By demonstrating the viability of the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater franchise on portable hardware, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (GBA) helped ensure the continued relevance of the *Tony Hawk* brand in the era of handheld gaming.

Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (GBA) is often contrasted favorably with earlier, less faithful adaptations of the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater series on the Game Boy Color, with critics describing Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (GBA) as "a more faithful version" and a "rather solid" entry in the handheld lineup.
Ultimately, *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance is remembered as a defining moment for the Game Boy Advance platform.

*Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance was not merely a competent port but a creative reinterpretation that respected the source material of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 while embracing the unique possibilities and constraints of the Game Boy Advance.

*Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance's success proved that developers could achieve remarkable graphical and mechanical fidelity on the handheld, inspiring a wave of more ambitious titles in the years that followed.

*Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance's legacy is one of innovation and influence, serving as a case study in how technical ingenuity and a deep understanding of a platform's capabilities could lead to the creation of a "hand-held gem" that remains celebrated decades after Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (GBA)'s release.

*Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2* for the Game Boy Advance remains a benchmark against which all other Game Boy Advance ports are measured, a testament to the vision of Vicarious Visions and the enduring appeal of the *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater* series.

4.content:
The dragon's first handheld adventure is a great first try with a bit of room for improvement.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

It's great to see developers attempt ambitious game designs now that the Game Boy Advance is out, because if the Game Boy Color was still king of the handheld ring I'm sure that [Universal Interactive](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025076.html) would have given Spyro's first portable adventure the usual, boring, generic side-scrolling treatment. But thanks to the GBA's upgraded hardware capabilities ,we're given a cool first attempt at an isometric platformer on the handheld in _[Spyro the Dragon: Season of Ice](https://gameboy.ign.com/objects/015/015445.html)_. The game is definitely a good one, but it's not without flaws...and with a few additions and a bit of tweaks it could have gone from good to great. But being good ain't that bad, you know?_Features_

*   More than 20 levels
*   Unlockable minigames
*   Battery Save (one save slot)
*   Only for Game Boy Advance

Seems all the fairies in the land have been encased in ice, and it up to our pal purple dragon Spyro to save the day (again) by freeing them out of their frigid prison. The Game Boy Advance version of Spyro's adventure attempts to mirror the structured gameplay of the PlayStation trilogy -- _Season of Ice_ is more of an exploration/collection game than a platformer. Oh, sure, you'll bound from ledge to ledge in certain places, but it's more about galloping around the area and locating gems and items, and the occasional crystalized fairy. These fairies aren't always out in the open, as in many instances in all of the game's levels, you have to perform tasks to get some characters to cough up a fairy of their own; in one level, for example, you'll have to ignite four lighthouses that are located in different areas of the beach level, or in another, headbutt a superfast thief in the merchant world. The tasks aren't incredibly tough to perform or figure out, it's just that you have to make sure that you've gone to every inch of the level to find everything that's necessary in completing them.To give the game a better feeling of 3D, Digital Eclipse designed an isometric scrolling engine so that Spyro can move freely in every direction. The look is something similar to what Vicarious Visions did in _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2_ on the GBA, and the same awkwardness that's in the skater is here in Spyro's adventure...players will have to adjust their eyes to understand the differing heights of all the surrounding ledges, because, other than Spyro's shadow, there isn't a good reference point to show which platforms are up high, and which ledges are separated by empty void. A lot of practice is necessary in order to learn the game's perspective, since players will have to use their jumping and gliding powers a lot in later levels.

The game doesn't use a 3D engine, so Spyro can't really "look ahead" in all directions like he can in the PlayStation designs to see gems, items, and areas a good distance away. The developers try to alleviate this downside with a simple command: hold down L and you can scroll the screen a short distance in each direction. But this isn't enough, unfortunately...and I never found a reason to use this function. Instead, what the developers could and should have done was to offer a full map of each level that could be pulled up at any time, showing where your dragon is in relation to the rest of the level. A lot of time is spent backtracking over certain parts of a world trying to find that one place you haven't traversed yet, and it's a little unfair to the gamer to "hide" level areas from view because the screen doesn't scroll far enough to see. This could have been addressed by implementing a "fog of war" type element on the non-existent level map, only revealing areas that have actually been explored.

But despite this overall design fault, the game itself is very well put together -- Digital Eclipse worked like the dickens creating different things to do in the same isometric engine, and there's plenty here to keep players going to the end. And it's good that the developers saw that there's only so much you can do in this perspective, as there are minigames to unlock that add a bit more to the variety. The overhead Sparx levels isn't much more than a version of Gauntlet, but it's a lot of fun and a good surprise for those not knowing about these challenges. And though the Spyro flying levels are a nice addition, the designers didn't pounce on the opportunity to push the GBA's abilities...instead of an ambitious flight game like _Pilotwings_, we get a really, really basic version of _Space Harrier_. I'd be lying if I said I wasn't disappointed in seeing and playing this minigame...it's okay, just nothing special.

### Verdict

I really do like Spyro the Dragon_. I think it's one of the better action games on the handheld...and with its cartridge battery saving everything in progress, it makes for a portable-friendly game as well. But the more I play the game, the more I see stuff that could have been improved on, and I'm hopeful that if and when it's time to create Spyro's portable sequel, the development team can fix and alter the game's obvious omissions and slight design compromises. As is, though, it's a good game with a lengthy quest and a decent challenge._

8.content:
We all know that _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater_ is a phenominal series on the consoles, but wait until you wrap your hands around a Game Boy Advance this June to play the portable version. _Tony Hawk Pro Skater 2_ could possibly go down as the top launch title for the system, even eclipsing Nintendo's own offerings on the GBA's release. If you haven't experienced the skating goodness, you really need to see the title in action to appreciate the work that's gone into the project -- [click here](https://pocket.ign.com/previews/16246.html) to head straight to our preview that includes video footage of THPS2 in action.But how did the portable gamecome about? How did [Activision](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025004.html) give life to the amazing handheld edition? We went right to the source of the Game Boy Advance version: [Vicarious Visions](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025232.html), the development team responsible for the Hawk's flight on GBA. Karthik Bala, CEO of Vicarious Visions and Matt Conte, Lead Programmer of [Tony Hawk 2](https://gameboy.ign.com/objects/016/016246.html) GBA helped answer our pressing questions about the stunning project.

**IGNpocket:** How long has Tony Hawk 2 been in development at Vicarious Visions? Is it the first project the you guys started on the Game Boy Advance?

**Karthik Bala:** Tony has been in development since August 2000. We got final approval on April 6th, so roughly 8 months in development. However, we have had AGB devkits since April 2000, so there was some R&D time before we officially started the project. Yep, it's our first project on the system.

**IGNpocket:** What was the design process in bringing Tony Hawk 2 to the Game Boy Advance? Was it always intended as a partial polygonal engine, or did it evolve that way?

**Karthik Bala:** Actually, there's a funny story on how the project started. After finishing Spider-Man GBC for Activision, we were looking to move onto Game Boy Advance. We thought about what obvious projects people would do on the AGB - SNES ports, Mode 7 racers etc. and decided to exactly not do that. Someone suggested Tony Hawk (it might have been our janitor) - and we realized it would be a lot of fun if that gameplay experience could be reproduced on a handheld. But it would be seriously tricky and high risk to pull off. Not to mention it's Activision's crown jewels.

During E3 last year, I came up with the idea of mocking up screenshots of what Tony \*could\* look like on AGB. It was assuming sprite based skater and I had an artist mock some pics up and FedEx color prints to me overnight at the show. I managed to get into Activision's booth, spotted the Man himself, and got one of the producers to show it to Tony. Tony was quite impressed and it went from there. We had a handshake deal with Activision by the end of the show. A bit of guerilla marketing, but it worked.

That was the easy part. When the programmers and artists figured out it would take over 100 megs of storage space to store all the animation frames at various discrete angles and rotations, using sprite based characters would be out of the question - if we wanted the player to perform every trick from the PSX version. Knowing that the system is a 2D system required us to write a software 3D engine. It was all speculation and theory at the time. Even if we got that to work, there was the little problem of the character skating on a 2D isometric bitmap and think it was all in 3D (complete with surface geometry definitions).

Thank God for the mysterious coding gnomes who do the night shift at VV! They worked really hard on this project and managed to solve all these problems for us.

**IGNpocket:** How close is the game's design to the 3D versions that are on the PlayStation, PC and Dreamcast? What had to be changed in order to get the game to work on the handheld?

**Karthik Bala:** The game design is very close to the PSX/DC version of the game. Some of the maps were redesigned to fit better within an isometric view, but we had the help of two awesome Activision testers who lived at VV for a few weeks to help redesign and tweak the levels for optimal play from this new POV. We knew we had reproduced the experience of Tony 2 PSX when players were doing 400,000 point combos and 1.5 million points in a 2 minute run!

**Matt Conte:** As development progressed, the game's design got closer and closer to the original PSX game. Knowing that there is a very definite benchmark of quality and playability attached to the THPS2 name, we tried to retain the look and feel of every aspect of the game. This did not come without its challenges, however.

The first challenge was the most obvious: how could we make the game play like the original? The fixed isometric angle proved to be the best for representing a true 3D world given our restrictions imposed by hardware and cartridge space. The decision to use a realtime-rendered polygonal character was the next big challenge overcome; this was our solution to fitting 7000+ frames of animation onto a cartridge that was little more than 1% of the size of a PlayStation disc.

To make the skating experience as playable and enjoyable as possible, and to retain the original feel of THPS2, all of the math for the physics is done in 3D. This was a significant challenge on the AGB, where the processor can't divide! Needless to say, there's a fair amount of heavily optimized assembly code powering the game. All of the surfaces you skate on are represented by mathematical equations, which reduced the amount of space level data required.

One of the most interesting problems we were faced with was obscuring the character behind objects that were in front of him, with regards to the camera. We had initially thought we could use features of the hardware to do this, but unfortunately because of limitations of the hardware, and the way we set up the graphics, we had to handle the character masking in software. What we ended up with looks really nice -- on the LCD screen, your character becomes semi-transparent when behind objects. And one of the biggest challenges was just fitting the dang thing onto the cart! There are tons of frames of animations, a huge amount of level graphics, and we still wanted to have rich music and SFX to complement the rest of the game.

**IGNpocket:** What's the music like in the game -- is it the licensed music from the console versions? Or are they original pieces? How's the sound capability in the system, generally speaking?

**Karthik Bala:** The music in the game is all original. Unfortunately there isn't enough cartridge space to store the licensed music. Shin'en (the Iridion 3D guys) did a fabulous job and did rewrite after rewrite to get the style and sound right on the AGB. Doing electric guitars on the hardware is tough!

**Matt Conte:** Our buddies over at Shin'en Multimedia did amazing work fitting some hardcore punk and rock onto the tiny cart!

**IGNpocket:** How is Neversoft involved in the Game Boy Advance version...or are they involved at all?

**Karthik Bala:** Neversoft checked out the game from time to time to see how it was progressing and have given us good feedback. And of course it was cool to get an email from Tony Hawk saying that the game rocks!

**IGNpocket:** The Game Boy Advance wasn't exactly made to be a 3D system. How far is Tony Hawk 2 pushing the system?

**Matt Conte:** As far as it will let us. Honestly though, that's kind of a misleading question, because there are different ways to really push the AGB. Because we are rendering the character, and we wanted to be able to zoom the entire screen and sprites for special effects, we gave up a lot of things that the hardware allows you to do for free. The AGB was definitely engineered with 2D games in mind; there are so many nice features that are available to the programmers and artists, that it is easily one of the most powerful 2D consoles I've ever seen. I think that it's a bit disappointing that most developers are concentrating on trying to engineer 3D technologies on the AGB; you just give up so many nice features that you would otherwise get to exploit. So I think in future games, we'll explore other avenues of game design where we can focus on using the hardware features a bit more,and push the little handheld even farther.

The AGB has a really nice sound system. It's very simple - it allows you to use the old GBC sound chip, plus it gives you two streaming PCM channels for digital audio. It looks like most titles are using a hybrid approach of the PCM channels plus the GBC soundchip for their music and effects. We've decided to NOT use the GBC sound chip, and budget more resources on sound and effects than most developers, for the simple reason that we feel most people are tired of the "blips" and "bleeps" attributed with chipmusic. We think the end user will appreciate this decision.

**IGNpocket:** Is there anything you wanted to put into Tony Hawk 2 GBA that couldn't get into the game's development whether it's hardware or time restrictions?

**Karthik Bala:** Oh, there was a bunch of stuff. The game is \*packed\* as is. Every last byte of cartridge space has been consumed. The main thing that we couldn't put in due to time restrictions was multiplayer. However, there's plenty of gameplay already in to keep even the die hard Tony Hawk fan busy.

**IGNpocket:** Activision has already announced Tony Hawk 3 for the Game Boy Advance ¿ will you guys be involved in that game's development?

**Karthik Bala:** I can't really comment on that. Suffice to say that we've had a blast working on Tony Hawk 2 and we got it done on time for launch. So, Activision seems to be happy with us.

**IGNpocket:** How has Nintendo handled third-party relations for Game Boy Advance development? Have they been helpful in working with you guys during your game development?

**Karthik Bala:** They've been good to work with so far. Early stages of the project was tough because there was a shortage of devkits, the tools were incomplete and the hardware was going through revisions. This is the case with any new system and it certainly makes development more uncertain than it usually is. But after seeing Tony for the first time, they were pretty jazzed about it and gave us the support we needed.

**IGNpocket:** What's your take on the Game Boy Advance system? Is it a good system, a limiting system? What things would you liked to have seen in the hardware design that weren't included?

**Karthik Bala:** It's a great system to work on. Really well designed. Vicarious Visions is certainly making Game Boy Advance a big part of our future development efforts.

**Matt Conte:** We are absolutely thrilled with the system. I don't think anyone was prepared for how powerful and capable the system really is. It continues to surprise us day in and day out.

**IGNpocket:** Are more publishers moving away from Game Boy Color development in favor of GBA? Or are companies still willing to fund GBC development?

**Karthik Bala:** Certainly publishers are moving in that direction. However, I suspect there will still be GBC titles coming out until the installed base of AGB gets large enough. Remember there's more than 100 million Game Boys out there. VV is currently working on new GBC titles and will be until the end of the year.

**IGNpocket:** What's next for you guys after GBA Tony Hawk 2 and GBA Spider-man? Anyone looking to use the Tony Hawk game engine other titles?

**Karthik Bala:** Well, we're putting the finishing touches to Spider-Man AGB , which takes what we did on Spidey GBC and cranks it up several notches on AGB. We have a gag order not to talk about our other titles in development, but all I can say is that one of our upcoming titles is \*big\* and should blow away what we've done so far. We're just starting to learn what the AGB can do and we're committed to keep pushing the hardware and create really great games.

As far as the Tony Hawk engine is concerned, the answer is yes.

_Interview by Craig Harris_

### Summary

Pull off a 50 or 50 grind, throw up a hand-plant, catch massive air, and stick a few ollies in this hand-held gem. You'll get your choice of 13 of the world's best skaters (including Tony Hawk, of course), as you move from street to park in this detailed update on the popular PRO SKATER series. No more incidents with the cops, skinned knees, stupid-looking helmets, or run-ins with street punks; this game brings you all of the action of real skating without any of the hang-ups. Cool graphics, a killer soundtrack, and epic gameplay make TONY HAWK'S PRO-SKATER 2 a must-have.

When it comes to the topic of titles that push the Game Boy Advance hardware, one game that constantly comes up is Vicarious Vision's **[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2](https://www.timeextension.com/features/games/gba/tony_hawks_pro_skater_2)**, and it's easy to see why.

Released as a launch title for the console in June 2001 in North America (and June 22nd in Europe), the game was an impressive adaptation of the popular PlayStation skateboarding title, which managed to surpass people's expectations. Tasked with creating something that emulated the 3D gameplay of the PlayStation original, Vicarious Visions didn't end up shying away from the challenge, opting not to produce a simple sidescroller similar to Natsume's earlier Game Boy Color port. Instead, the studio decided to split the difference, settling upon an isometric viewpoint featuring a real-time rendered 3D character that ran on much of the same source code as the original.

At the time, it's safe to say that the vast majority of journalists and gamers were pretty blown away at what Vicarious Visions had managed to pull off, with many of them believing that Nintendo's new device had only been capable of outputting 2D sprite-based graphics. Because of this, it went on to receive some incredible reviews from publications like [IGN](https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/06/14/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2-9), [Gamespot](https://www.gamespot.com/reviews/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2-review/1900-2770362/), and Next Generation, in addition to winning several awards (including a BAFTA for "Best Mobile Interactive Game") and spawning a bunch of other games using the same technology and approach.

So, with all that in mind, we felt it was about time to do a proper deep dive into the development of what is now considered a handheld classic and look at some of the challenges Vicarious Visions faced and how it overcame them. So we reached out to Matt Conte, the lead programmer on the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 port, who was happy to go into detail about how the game was made, and even gave us some info on Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3, which he also worked on.

### New Hardware, New Challenges

According to the previous accounts we've come across, Vicarious Visions first had the idea of making a Tony Hawk's game when work on their Game Boy Color **[Spiderman](https://www.timeextension.com/features/games/gbc/spider-man)** title for the publisher Activision was winding down.

In April 2000, Nintendo had presented the company with a bunch of AGB devkits for developing games for the as-yet-to-be-released Game Boy Advance handheld, which had led Vicarious Visions to come up with a list of potential games it could create for the handheld.

According to Vicarious Visions CEO Karthik Bala [in a 2001 IGN interview](https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/05/04/interview-with-the-tony-hawk-2-gba-team), the studio considered working SNES ports, Mode 7-style racers, and other similar titles, but eventually someone suggested making a port of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 for the handheld instead. This ended up capturing people's imagination, with different members of the studio getting excited over what this might look like. So the decision was made to try and go after the license.

By this point in time, Vicarious Visions already had a close relationship with Activision, thanks to working on Spiderman, but those inside the studio knew that getting to work on Tony Hawk would likely prove to be difficult. The publisher considered Tony Hawk to be one of its crown jewels and wasn't about to just give it out to anyone. So, as a result, Vicarious Vision's CEO Karthik Bala came up with a plan during E3 in May 2000 to have the lead artist Andy Lomerson create a bunch of mockups of what a Tony Hawk game could look like using the AGB hardware.

The intention was then to fax these over to Bala at the event and to present them to Tony Hawk on the show floor. That way Tony Hawk and Activision would be able to see for themselves what a game could look like, without having to spend any funds towards its development.

Speaking about how the team arrived at this isometric view, Conte states, "We kind of sat down and said, ‘Well, how can we translate this to GBA in a way that feels authentic?’ Because we didn’t want to rewrite the entire game. So we started formulating a plan of ‘Okay, there’s no way we can make a full 3D representation. We can’t emulate what’s happening on PSX.’ So we kind of settled on this projection which we felt could give most of the feeling of the level layouts and access to most of the level components.

"Even if you took all of the levels and flipped them so you were looking at a top-down perspective, most of the level geometry and all of the level components are accessible in that view. So we felt that the isometric projection would work especially well given the tile-based graphics system on the Game Boy Advance. So that would be a good approach forward."

[![Image 5: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2](https://images.timeextension.com/95bb6dbfdc367/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2.900x.jpg)](https://images.timeextension.com/95bb6dbfdc367/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2.large.jpg "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2")

One of the changes in the Hangar level in the GBA version is that players will no longer have to smash through a pane of glass to access the second half of the stage featuring the attack helicopter — _Image: Vicarious Visions/Activision_

Remarkably, this canny bit of self-promotion managed to work, and Activision ended up striking a handshake agreement with the studio to develop the port of the game by the end of the event. After some formalities, development officially began a few months later, in August 2000, with the team diving headfirst into the project to try to make a game that felt worthy of the Tony Hawk name.

As this was the studio's first Game Boy Advance title, the team didn't have an advanced engine with a sophisticated level editor on hand. Instead, everything was mostly handled by math, with the programmers on the project having to manually set the point values for tiles in the environment to give them the desired amount of depth. This would allow them to create the simple level geometry.

"We obviously didn't have the computational ability or the memory or the ROM budget to build an entire 3D polygonal world," says Conte. "So, the way that the engine worked was basically a height map. So if you took the isometric projection and you rotated it so that you're just looking at a grid from like top down, for every particular point that you could choose, you would say X, Y, and then you would get a Z value. You'd get a height.

"And the way that we did that was using parametric functions. So, you know, if you were on a flat plane, it was simple. You would just say z is 0 or z is 10 or something like that. For a quarter pipe, it was a quadratic equation. So we would try and approximate the curvature based on x, y and we would find out the z based on this quadratic equation."

As for the skater, the team also found themselves having to write new software, to achieve the 3D effect they wanted. Originally, while putting together the initial mockups, they had been intending to use digitized sprites for the project. These are pre-rendered 3D models that have been converted into sprites before being implemented in the game. However, once they had access to Neversoft's source code, they soon realized that the number of individual frames of animation for the various tricks and maneuvers was somewhere in the thousands and it wouldn't be possible to store all that on a single GBA cartridge. Instead, the team would have to come up with another solution.

"We just did the math and we said, ‘Okay if we’re going to allow you to go omnidirectional in this isometric world, there is no room on the cartridge for us to store every single frame of those 5000 frames at 8 or 16 or 32 arbitrary directions.’ So the other programmer, Alex \[Rybakov\], had some experience with some real-time 3D rendering back in the day, on PC games, and so he spent maybe a month or a month and a half prototyping a real-time renderer that was Gouraud shaded. So it wasn’t flat-shaded.

"So in pretty short order, we had a prototype of a 3D render that would work within, I believe, a 64x64 sprite that we could then layer on top of the game field." Discovering how to render the skater wasn't the end of the problems, however.

### Animation, Music, & Recapturing The Magic

As Conte tells us, there was also the issue of how to emulate the feel of the classic Tony Hawk games on the Nintendo handheld.

In its initial planning, Vicarious Visions had intended to reuse much of the original Neversoft source code, to ensure the experience felt as close to the PlayStation version as possible, but Neversoft's source code was almost entirely written in C++ and Nintendo had stated in the official documentation accompanying the AGB dev kit that the device could only be coded in C. Because of this, Conte had to convince Nintendo it was possible to develop for the console to run C++, or risk having to convert everything over himself.

"I was like, 'I'm not gonna port however many hundred thousands of lines of code over to sort of a precursor language,'" he tells us. "So, I put together a proof of concept and made it work on the GBA. And I ended up giving sort of a presentation to them, which became a blog post on their internal site about, 'Here's how you can make C++ work on the GBA'. So with that sort of out of the way, we could then start on actually porting the bulk of the PSX code over to the GBA."

[![Image 10: YouTube Video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/E5NRhPlRQQU/maxresdefault.jpg)Watch on **YouTube**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E5NRhPlRQQU "Play")

According to Conte, reusing the code was one of the key reasons why the physics in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 feels so accurate to the original. This apparently didn't just apply to the physics either, with Conte stating that much of the "trick script" Neversoft wrote was also repurposed for the handheld version.

"Trick script was basically a very rudimentary scripting language that they gave their designers to design the tricks and it was like super simple commands such as start this animation or play a sound if you do a nutter. And the interesting thing with TrickScript was that it was actually converted into a binary language, which was created by the PlayStation 1 assembler. So this is what PSX programmers would use to create assembly language binaries.

"And then in the runtime, like in the actual code, there was like a C++ code that would basically decode that. It was basically like byte code. It would read a byte and then start a trick and see this is the point value or, you know, this is the length of the trick and it would just sort of like loop through that. So, to basically shortcut the process of converting all that over, I just took the PlayStation assembler executable and used that to create a binary. So we're basically using PlayStation tools to create byte code that we would then execute on the GBA."

With the team gradually overcoming most of the technical hurdles in their way, there was still another pressing question that needed to be answered: how the music in the game would be handled.

The Tony Hawk's Pro Skater games were at that point well known for their use of licensed bands. However, using pre-existing recordings was simply not possible on the handheld as there wouldn't be enough room on the cartridge to store all of the sampled tracks. Because of this, Vicarious Visions reached out to the German composer and former demoscener Manfred Linzner, who had previously collaborated with the studio on Spiderman to see what he could come up with.

[![Image 11: YouTube Video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/dmpoBJ5UMb0/maxresdefault.jpg)Watch on **YouTube**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dmpoBJ5UMb0 "Play")

"I forget even how much the cartridge ROM was on Tony 2 but we knew that we weren't gonna be able to do like full sample tracks," says Conte. "I think some other titles came out later that were able to use sample tracks, but like we just didn't have the space given all the level data and the animation data we were gonna be eating up.

"So we basically approached Manfred and said you know 'We would like you to kind of create like a pastiche, or songs that are in the style of Tony Hawk tracks.' And like, it's kind of nice in the Tony series there isn't a particular track that is associated with a particular level. Most of the work that I had done with him before, like on the Spider-Man game, was 'Okay, you're down in the sewer, you need kind of like this eerie kind of sound.' But this time we just said, 'We have the space on the cartridge for you to build these songs. Here are the tracks from the original soundtrack and here are some other songs that we kind of picked ourselves from skate punk-type artists. Try and build something similar.'

The result of this collaboration was a 10-song soundtrack that includes plenty of distortion-heavy skate-punk tracks, as well as a couple of funkier hip-hop-inspired tunes. These work together to capture the spirit of the original and are all available to be selected from the pause menu at any time, regardless of the current level.

### The Road To Release & Creating A Legacy

As all of the different components were coming together, Vicarious Visions started compiling builds to send over to the Activision QA team to test, but the initial feedback wasn't quite as enthusiastic as what the team had been expecting. In fact, Activision's workers heavily criticized the level layouts, believing that while the game certainly looked the part and was technically impressive, it was lacking some of the purposeful level design that had been present in the original PS1 title.

As Conte recalls, "We had started sending it to Activision's QA team. And they had a team that was entirely focused on Tony Hawk, and the Tony Hawk series. So like these guys played Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 like all day, every day, as their job. And so, we gave them an early version to get some feedback about it and they tore it apart.

"They were like, 'This is all wrong.' Like the technology's great, things look great, but 'You guys don't understand how to build levels at all.' And we basically brought them on full-time, kind of as consultants, to help us understand the language of what makes a Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 level. Like how this rail has to line up with that funbox and how you create these lines. Everything is set up with a purpose in the PlayStation levels and we had kind of missed that in our attempt to recreate the looks of the levels in the isometric projection and moving stuff around."

Because of this, the team ended up going through all of the levels again to give them another pass, paying particular attention to how they rewarded high-level play and creating better lines to allow players to chain together a greater combination of tricks on the fly. This turned out to be one of the final ingredients, in their quest to make the game feel just as satisfying as the original.

All in all, the game took less than a year to develop from the very start of production to when it finally hit store shelves in June 2001 and was greeted upon release with a ton of enthusiastic press from video game journalists. For the team, this was a major relief, but not entirely surprising as they knew that what they had set out was unlike anything else on the system.

Conte states, "We knew that with it being a launch title, there was not a whole lot else on the plate, to begin with, and the quality usually evolves from what launches on day zero versus a few years into its lifetime. So I don't think we were super surprised at the response. It also had the Tony Hawk IP attached to it, and Tony was huge at that time. So it felt like a winning combination."

In the aftermath of Tony Hawk Pro Skater 2, Vicarious Visions later ended up updating and reusing its 3D renderer for various other projects it was working on, including **[Crash Bandicoot: The Huge Adventure](https://www.timeextension.com/features/games/gba/crash_bandicoot_the_huge_adventure)**, Jet Grind Radio, and Tony Hawk Pro Skater 3. In the case of Tony Hawk Pro Skater 3, one of the biggest changes was the creation of an actual 3D-level editor, to allow the developers to design stages more intuitively.

Speaking about this editor, Conte recalls, "It looked like what Unity or something looks like today. You could rotate everything around, and place a rail from here to there. You could set up where the gaps were. You could set up the points where the escape letters were. All that stuff. So that was all custom built."

In addition to this, there were other changes too, with the character no longer being Gouraud shaded, but texture-mapped instead. This allowed the team to implement features like more detailed clothing and a create-a-skater option, whereby players could tweak the attire of existing skateboarders or create their very own character from scratch. The team also introduced 4-player multiplayer using the link cable (a feature that had been removed from the previous game during development), allowing players to experience games like H-O-R-S-E, Tag, King of the Hill, and Trick Attack.

Similar to its predecessor, Tony Hawk Pro Skater 3 ended up receiving some stellar reviews from video game outlets, with [IGN awarding it a 9.6 out of 10](https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/03/06/tony-hawks-pro-skater-3), calling it "an incredible package" and "a lot deeper than you're led to believe". Meanwhile, Gamespot gave it a 9.5, stating it was perhaps "[the only Game Boy Advance game to truly usurp Tony Hawk 2](https://www.gamespot.com/reviews/tony-hawks-pro-skater-3-review/1900-2853831/)".

Following Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3's release, Vicarious Visions inevitably went on to work on more Game Boy Advance ports of Tony Hawk's console games, contributing to pretty much all of them except 2006's **[Downhill Jam](https://www.timeextension.com/features/games/gba/tony_hawks_downhill_jam)**, which was handled by the company Visual Impact (Vicarious Visions would be tasked instead with creating Downhill Jam's Nintendo DS port). Its relationship with Tony Hawk didn't stop there either, with the company later developing **Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2** for PCs and consoles in 2020.

Today, whenever anyone mentions Vicarious Visions' Tony Hawk Pro Skater games for the Game Boy Advance in conversation, it's usually accompanied by total disbelief at what the studio managed to achieve with the limited hardware that was available to them. The games remain highly playable to this day and are still some of the best action sports titles that are available for the handheld.

Nice interview, I'm a huge THPS fan, and I also love the GBA, so this was a great read for me. I had no idea that they actually used PSone code on a GBA, I just assumed they built the game from scratch, but it makes sense now, seeing as how well the games control, compared to the awful Robomodo games which were built from scratch and played terribly.

THPS 2 was an amazing GBA launch game, and the main system seller for me, THPS 3 was also great, THPS 4 was good too, but it was starting to feel stale by then (not on consoles, but on GBA with its more limited game design).

Fortunately for me, at that point PSP had launched with THUG 2 Remix, now the GBA games had lost their luster and charm. I finally had a 'true 3D' THPS game to play on the go. So I stopped buying the GBA games from then on. However I recently went back to play them via emulation just to see what I had missed.

THUG GBA was horrible, they completely ruined it, THUG 2 GBA was okay, but that feeling of staleness was certainly increasing, THAW GBA is similar to THUG 2, but worse with some stupid goals that aren't well explained to the player. Overall the games were going downhill in quality after THPS 4.

The last game, Downhill Jam on GBA was extremely impressive for the hardware, can you imagine what it would have been like to see a game like that on GBA's launch? It would have been insane! Perhaps you should interview someone who worked on that game? Also Downhill Jam on DS is amazing, and is well worth a try.

Version Updates
=============================================================================

Final Version - Sephy Kid (the creator of the THPS2 Gaps guide has allowed me 
to include his gap guide in this guide.  Also, many grammatical errors have 
been corrected.  This guide covers almost every aspect of this game and will 
not be updated again.

Version 2.03 - Added another method to 50-50 Joey's Sculpture (thanks to Per

Version 0.3 - Added information on deck statistics (thanks to Nintendork).

Version 0.2 - Completed the deck listing for Tony Hawk and Spiderman.  Some

Version 0.1 - This is the first version of the walkthrough which contains the

=============================================================================
1.   Introduction                                                  thps2_1000
=============================================================================

I choose to create a guide for the Game Boy Advance version of Tony Hawk's 
Pro Skater 2 because I believe it is the best Game Boy Advance launch title.  

When making this guide, I realized it is difficult to describe the locations 
of items in the courses in this game.  Please keep these few things in mind 
when reading this FAQ.  When it is stated that an item is located above 
something (quarter pipe, ramp, rail, etc.) it means that you must jump (or 
ollie) to get the item.  When describing locations to direct your skater, I 
do so based on the gamer's perspective (not the skater's).  Also, you must 
keep in mind that Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 has a 3/4 overhead perspective and 
the courses are displayed at a 45° angle not a 0° angle.  For example, when 
an item is located to the right of something it is actually located right + 
45° of something.  If you still don't understand:

--------------->  (Right)

     /\ Approximately right + 45° (ASCII art has its limitations)
     /
    /
   /
  /
 /
/

The same 45° addition applies for all directions.  If you still don't 
understand, get a compass. Or look at this ASCII one:

                     North (normal top)
                       |  
(top + 45°) Northwest  | Northeast (right + 45°)
                     \ | /
                      \|/
     West -------------|-------------- East (normal right)
(normal left)         /|\
                     / | \
            Southwest  |  Southeast (bottom + 45°)
       (left + 45°)    |
                     South
                (normal bottom)

This guide uses a "code location" system.  This means that there are special 
key codes throughout this guide that can be used to navigate through the 
large amount of text quickly.  The key code numbers for a desired section of 
this guide are located in the Table of Contents.  To jump to an area of the 
guide quickly, simply use the find command (usually Ctrl + F) in Notepad or 
your web browser and enter thps2_#### (where #### is the location code).  I 
did not invent this idea; it has been used on many other text-based gaming 
guides before.

=============================================================================
2.   Game Basics                                                   thps2_2000
=============================================================================

-------------
The Controls:
-------------

Up:           Lean Forward, Exit Pool, Manual Balance
Down:         Brake, Lean Back, Manual Balance
Left & Right: Turn, Grind Balance
B:            Crouch, Ollie
A:            Grind
L:            Flip Trick, Toggle Nollie
R:            Grab Trick, Switch
Start:        Pause Game
Select:       Not used

--------------------
Control Information:
--------------------

The skater will always be moving forward.  Press the B button will make the 
skater crouch and increase in speed.  

When turning, the skater will turn to its left or right, not left or right on 
the screen.

Pressing and holding the DOWN button on the control pad will cause the skater 
to slow down and eventually stop.

An ollie is preformed when the B button is released.  The longer the B button 
is held down, the higher the ollie.

A nollie is preformed when the L button is tapped (putting the skater in the 
nollie position) and the B button is released.

A No Comply is preformed when UP is tapped once and the B button is released.

A Boneless is preformed when UP is tapped twice and the B button is released.

Manuals are preformed when UP then DOWN is pressed.  To keep balance, use the 
UP and DOWN buttons.  Pressing DOWN then UP will perform a nose manual.

Pressing the R button will change the skater's stance.

To make a landing from a big drop, press and hold the B button until impact.  
If you fall, hit the buttons on the control pad to get up quickly.

To perform a grind, press the A button when in the air close to an edge, rail 
or lip.  Pressing a direction on the control pad an A will perform different 
grinds.  

To perform a wallride, press B to jump, then hold A near a wall, sign or 
building when airborne.  When approaching a wall, the skater should be almost 
parallel to the wall. 

Lip tricks are preformed by skating up a ramp while holding the A button and 
a direction on the control pad.

Pressing the L button and a direction when airborne preforms flip tricks.  

Pressing the R button and a direction when airborne preforms grab tricks.

--------
Scoring:
--------

The scoring system in Tony Hawk's is very complex.  Here is some basic 
information that will help you achieve better scores.  Performing more than 
one stunt in the same jump will increase your score.  Performing more than 
one trick on the same jump is called a trick string.  Completing a trick the 
first time will give you 100% of its point value.  

Each successive time the trick is preformed its point value will decrease.  
The second time a trick is performed you will earn 75% of its point value.  
The third time, the trick will receive 50% of its total point value.  The 
fourth time, the trick will receive 25% of its total point value.  The fifth 
time, the trick will receive 10% of its total point value.

Grinds, manuals, lip tricks and grabs all have a score associated them.  
These base scores can be held longer to acquire additional points.

Spinning during trick strings will multiply your score.  When spinning 180° 
the multiplier will increase.  A 180° spin will multiply your score by 1.5x.  
A 360° spin will multiply your score by 2.0x.  A 540° spin will multiply your 
score by 3.0x.  A 720° spin will multiply your score by 4.0x.  Finally, A 
900° spin will multiply your score by 6.0x.

Your landing will also affect your score.  Landing a perfect trick will give 
you 150% percent of the trick's score.  Landing a sloppy trick gives you 75% 
of the trick's score.

=============================================================================
3.   Skaters                                                       thps2_3000
=============================================================================

Each skater has different default statistics.  These statistics reflect their 
own unique skating style.  Earning cash in the career mode can improve 
statistics with a number rating.  The maximum rating for a character 
statistic is 10.  

Each character has three default special moves and space for three more 
additional special moves.  These moves can be bought by earning cash in the 
career mode.

The Skate Shop is used to upgrade a character's skateboard.  In the Skate 
Shop you can modify your deck and trucks.  The trucks affect the turning 
statistic and the deck affects the weight, speed and durability statistics.  
Turning, weight, speed and durability all have a minimum value of 1 and a 
maximum value of 5.

Deck statistics change based on the amount of decks you purchase.  Each 
character has the same amount of decks.  The following chart will explain the 
changes in board statistics:
 ___________________________________________________________________________
|                                                                           |
|Statistics                   Number of Boards Purchased                    |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|                 0       1       2       3       4       5       6         |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Weight           1       2       2       3       4       4       5         |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Speed            1       1       2       2       3       5       5         |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Durability       1       1       1       3       4       4       5         |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Cost            $0     $250    $500    $750    $1000   $1250   $1500       |
|___________________________________________________________________________|

There are three kinds of trucks.  They affect a skater's turning ability.  
All three different kinds of trucks are available at the start and are free.  
Tight trucks have a turning value of 1.  Medium trucks have a turning value 
of 3.  Loose trucks have a turning value of 5.

============
a. Tony Hawk                                                       thps2_3001
============

If you meet Hawk, look at his shins.  You'll see how much flesh he's left 
behind becoming the most influential skateboarder in history.  He lost some 
perfecting the first 900°.  More went while creating 50+ signature moves and 
winning 12 world championships.  The father to two boys and modern 
skateboarding, Tony makes his home in his native SoCal.  (Character Bio taken 
from the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 instruction booklet.)

================
b. Bob Burnquist                                                   thps2_3002
================

Out of Brazil and onto the winner's podium, Bob Burnquist is one of today's 
most exciting and original skaters.  Blowing minds with his unique style and 
switch-stance tendencies, Burnquist won the first pro contest he entered.  He 
then went on to be the first skater to pull off an Eggplant Revert, a move 
now simply  known as the "Burntwist."  (Character Bio taken from the Tony 
Hawk's Pro Skater 2 instruction booklet.)

==================
c. Steve Caballero                                                 thps2_3003
==================

How long has Steve Caballero been part of the skateboarding scene?  Over 
three decades.  Along the way he helped found the Bones Brigade, invented the 
Cabbalerial and owned his share of world records - including the highest 
halfpipe air and 44-stair rail.  Cab's still riding hard, inspiring 
skateboarding's next generation.  (Character Bio taken from the Tony Hawk's 
Pro Skater 2 instruction booklet.)
