_**Tony Hawk's**_ is a series of [skateboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skateboarding "Skateboarding") video games published by [Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision "Activision") and endorsed by the [American professional skateboarder of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk "Tony Hawk"). From 1999 to 2007, the series was primarily developed for [home consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_video_game_console "Home video game console") by [Neversoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neversoft "Neversoft") with generally annual releases. In 2008, Activision transferred the franchise to Robomodo, which released several additions, before Activision and Hawk's license expired in 2015, leaving the future of the series uncertain.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-VR/Expired-1) In 2020, the series returned under Activision with a [remake of the original two games in the series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_1_%2B_2 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2"), and a remake of the third and fourth games in 2025 developed by [Vicarious Visions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicarious_Visions "Vicarious Visions") and [Iron Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Galaxy "Iron Galaxy") respectively.

Starting with _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_/(video_game/) "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater (video game)")_ in 1999,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Fielder-2) the series was one of the [best-selling video game franchises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_video_game_franchises "List of best-selling video game franchises") of the early 2000s. Three more _Pro Skater_ games were released from 2000 to 2002, after which the developers took a more story-oriented approach with the releases of _[Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground "Tony Hawk's Underground")_, _[Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2 "Tony Hawk's Underground 2"),_ and _[American Wasteland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_American_Wasteland "Tony Hawk's American Wasteland")_ from 2003 to 2005. _[Project 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Project_8 "Tony Hawk's Project 8")_ in 2006 and _[Proving Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Proving_Ground "Tony Hawk's Proving Ground")_ in 2007 were the final games in the series developed by Neversoft. Developer Robomodo took the franchise in a different direction with the [peripheral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peripheral "Peripheral")\-supported spin-offs _[Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Ride "Tony Hawk: Ride")_ and _[Shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Shred "Tony Hawk: Shred")_, released in 2009 and 2010 to critical reviews and poor sales. Robomodo tried to revive the series with the back-to-the-roots _[Pro Skater HD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_HD "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater HD")_ in 2012 and _[Pro Skater 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_5 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5")_ in 2015. The series spawned several other spin-offs, such as _[Downhill Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Downhill_Jam "Tony Hawk's Downhill Jam")_ in 2006 and _[Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Motion "Tony Hawk's Motion")_ in 2008, and several ports and re-releases.

Neversoft's first five _Tony Hawk's_ received critical acclaim for their unique gameplay, varied soundtracks, and expansion over their predecessors. _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2_ and _Pro Skater 3_ are ranked among the best games released for the [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_/(console/) "PlayStation (console)") and [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"), respectively.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-MC-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GSpot-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PS2-5) Later entries drew less favorable reviews; _Ride_ and _Pro Skater 5_ were named "Worst Games of the Year" by several outlets.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamesradar.com-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto1-8) After this, Activision let the licensing deal expire while holding all publishing rights.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-VR/Expired-1)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Wired-9) Fans continued to support the series through an [online multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_multiplayer "Online multiplayer") [fangame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fangame "Fangame") called _[THUG Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THUG_Pro "THUG Pro")_, which uses _[Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2 "Tony Hawk's Underground 2")_'s engine in an all-encompassing collection of levels from the series.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-hester1-10)

The first game bearing the _Tony Hawk's_ name not published by Activision, _[Tony Hawk's Skate Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Skate_Jam "Tony Hawk's Skate Jam")_, was released in December 2018 for [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS") and [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_/(operating_system/) "Android (operating system)").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-toucharcade.com-11) A second high-definition remake of the first two games, _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_1_%2B_2 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2")_, published by Activision and developed by [Vicarious Visions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicarious_Visions "Vicarious Visions") (who previously developed ports of several _Tony Hawk's_ games), was released in 2020.

The _Tony Hawk's_ series was originally developed as a classic [arcade game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game"). The goal of most modes of the game is to achieve a high score.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-20) To do this, the player must perform [aerials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_/(skateboarding/) "Aerial (skateboarding)"), [flips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flip_trick "Flip trick"), [grinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grind_/(skateboarding/) "Grind (skateboarding)"), [lips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lip_trick "Lip trick"), and [manuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freestyle_skateboarding_tricks#Manual "Freestyle skateboarding tricks"), with successful combinations adding to the player's score. The point value of the trick is based on time maintained, degrees rotated, number of tricks performed in sequence, performing tricks on specific landmarks on the map, and the number of times the tricks have been used.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-21) Successful tricks also add to the player's special meter, which, once full, allows the execution of special tricks that are worth a great deal more than normal tricks. Bails (falling off the skateboard due to poor landing) forfeit points for the attempted trick and reset the special bar to empty. The controls of the game developed as the series progressed. While the original _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater")_ featured a fairly limited set of moves, later entries allowed the player to switch between moves during the same grind or manual sequence, perform transfers, hold on to and drive various vehicles, walk on foot and scale walls, [slow time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_motion "Slow motion"), or perform more advanced tricks by pressing buttons repeatedly—for example, a double or triple [kickflip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickflip "Kickflip") instead of a normal one.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-22) Later entries, such as _[American Wasteland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_American_Wasteland "Tony Hawk's American Wasteland")_, allowed the player to use a [BMX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMX "BMX"), and _[Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Motion "Tony Hawk's Motion")_ and _[Shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Shred "Tony Hawk: Shred")_ featured [snowboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowboarding "Snowboarding").

The first three _Pro Skater_ games centered around an arcade mode, in which the player tries to achieve a high score, perform certain tasks, and collect a number of [objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collectable "Collectable") in a limited amount of time. If the player completes enough of these [objectives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quest_/(gaming/) "Quest (gaming)") in one [level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_/(video_gaming/) "Level (video gaming)"), they unlock other levels and acquire currency, with which they can improve their character. Competition levels require the player to gain an excellent score with minimal bails to progress.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-23) Starting with _[Pro Skater 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_2 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2")_, it became possible to create a custom character and design [skateparks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skatepark "Skatepark"). All games until _[Pro Skater 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_5 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5")_ featured [local multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_multiplayer "Local multiplayer"), while it was possible to compete in [online multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_multiplayer "Online multiplayer") since _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_3 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3")_. Since the first _Pro Skater_, it was possible to access all levels without having to perform tasks and without a time limit. This concept was later used in career mode from _[Pro Skater 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_4 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4")_ onwards.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-24) [Non-player characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character "Non-player character") give tasks to the player, who could otherwise freely explore the levels without time constraints. Starting with _[Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground "Tony Hawk's Underground")_, the series replaced the career mode with a story mode. In _Underground_, _[Project 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Project_8 "Tony Hawk's Project 8")_, and _[Proving Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Proving_Ground "Tony Hawk's Proving Ground")_, the story centered around the [player character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Player_character "Player character") turning into a [professional skateboarder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skateboarding "Skateboarding").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-25) In _[Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2 "Tony Hawk's Underground 2")_, the only direct [sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequel "Sequel") in the series, the player embarks on a destruction tour around the world, orchestrated by [Tony Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk "Tony Hawk") and [Bam Margera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bam_Margera "Bam Margera").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-26) In _American Wasteland_, the first of the series to feature one consecutive [open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") instead of separate levels, the player character aims to rebuild an old skatepark in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-27)

After [Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision "Activision") took the series from [Neversoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neversoft "Neversoft"), the new developer Robomodo changed the general outlet and gameplay of the franchise. _[Tony Hawk: Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Ride "Tony Hawk: Ride")_ and its successor, _[Tony Hawk: Shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Shred "Tony Hawk: Shred")_ introduced a [peripheral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peripheral "Peripheral") [skateboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skateboard "Skateboard") which replaced the [controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_controller "Game controller"). To provide a realistic skateboarding experience, turning, leaning, hopping, and other actions on the peripheral device were directly translated into the movements of the in-game character via [infrared sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_sensor "Infrared sensor"). This resulted in the abandonment of open levels, which were replaced by linear levels that had the character skate on pre-set paths. A similar attempt was made with the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") game _[Tony Hawk's Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Motion "Tony Hawk's Motion")_, which used a peripheral device that recognized the leaning of the DS system and had the skater move accordingly.

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Tony_Hawk_right_profile.jpg/250px-Tony_Hawk_right_profile.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tony_Hawk_right_profile.jpg)

Tony Hawk, the series' namesake, in 2006

To capitalize on the growing popularity of skateboarding as a sport, [Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision "Activision") approached small developer [Neversoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neversoft "Neversoft") to develop a skateboarding game. According to an interview with one of the developers in 2018, Activision originally wanted a skateboard [racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_game "Racing game") similar to [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega")'s [arcade game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game") _[Top Skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Skater "Top Skater")_, but after Neversoft showed them what their engine was capable of, the racing idea was abandoned in favor of a more free-flowing approach.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GameBrain_Interview-31) Activision signed professional skateboarder [Tony Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk "Tony Hawk") as the face of the skateboarding game _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_/(video_game/) "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater (video game)")_. The game had been in development long before Hawk was signed as the face of the brand; as such, his name and likeness were included late in development.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Barton_2-32) Originally, Hawk signed a [licensing contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/License "License") valid until 2002, which was then renewed until 2015, following the success of the _Pro Skater_ series.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-33) [Mitch Lasky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Lasky "Mitch Lasky"), at that time the senior vice president of Activision, stated in an interview with [GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot") that the game as well as the character were meant "to reflect Tony's signature style – an intense mix of acrobatics and hard-core technical skating". Hawk himself was involved in the development of the game and his in-game persona, remarking that "\[he had\] always wanted to help create a video game that represented the reality and excitement of professional skateboarding".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-air-34) Hawk, along with other skaters featured in the game, was animated for the game using [motion capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_capture "Motion capture")[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Fielder-2) and voiced his character.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-35)

### Neversoft era (1999–2007)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Hawk%27s&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Neversoft era (1999–2007)")\]

In early 1998, [Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision "Activision") approached by developer [Neversoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neversoft "Neversoft") to develop a skateboarding [racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_game "Racing game"), in order to capitalize on the growing popularity of the sport. The idea of a racing game was abandoned in development after Neversoft showed the adaptability of the control engine to various maneuvers.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GameBrain_Interview-31) Members of the team were fans of Sega's _[Top Skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Skater "Top Skater")_, which they played at a local arcade, and that served as a basic influence on the game's original concept, but _Top Skater_ had a racing element, which the team moved away from as they began studying real-life skaters.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Retro_Gamer-36) To make the gameplay seem as real as possible, company founder Joel Jewett had a [halfpipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halfpipe "Halfpipe") built in his backyard and started skateboarding with his coworkers.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Era-37) Also, [motion capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_capture "Motion capture") was used to make the skateboarding moves seem as realistic as possible.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Fielder-2) To distance the franchise from other games, the developers opted for licensing modern rock songs, in contrast to the classic music usual for video games at that time.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Era-37) The first game was developed within a year by a 12-person team,[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Era-37) and Tony Hawk was added as the face of the franchise late in development.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Barton_2-32) A month before the release of _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_/(video_game/) "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater (video game)")_ for [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_/(console/) "PlayStation (console)") in 1999, Hawk successfully performed a [900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/900_/(skateboarding/) "900 (skateboarding)") at that year's [X Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_Games "X Games"), which resulted in huge press coverage of the sport and helped boost sales.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Era-37) Also, the inclusion of the game on the _[Jampack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jampack "Jampack")_ [demo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_demo "Game demo") for the PlayStation generated further hype, as players were overwhelmed by the unique gameplay.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GameBrain_Interview-31) The huge success of the game prompted Neversoft to vastly expand its production staff in order to be able to release _Tony Hawk's_ games on a yearly basis.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Era-37) Neversoft held true to that ambition and released _[Pro Skater 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_2 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2")_ and _[Pro Skater 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_3 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3")_ in 2000 and 2001, respectively. Both games retained mostly the same gameplay as their predecessor, along with some improvements. The two games were the most critically acclaimed games for their respective consoles and still rank among the highest rated games of all time.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-MC-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GSpot-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PS2-5) Furthermore, _Pro Skater 3_ was the first [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2") game to feature online gameplay. Also, _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_2x "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x")_, a compilation of the first two games, was released as a launch title for the [Xbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_/(console/) "Xbox (console)") in 2001. 2002 saw the release of _[Pro Skater 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_4 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4")_; by this time, the franchise was among the best-selling video game franchises in the world.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-38) This was reflected in the manpower Activision and Neversoft invested in the franchise, as the employees working on the game had grown from 12 for the first entry to 150[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Era-37) and there were significantly more skaters featured, all of which received considerable royalties.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-The_Andrew_Reynolds_Interview-39)

With the 2003 release of the fifth entry in the series, _[Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground "Tony Hawk's Underground")_, the developers used storytelling and exploration to distance their product from the plotless, task-based format of the previous _Tony Hawk's_ games, which led Neversoft president Joel Jewett to describe _Underground_ as an adventure game.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-handson-40) It follows the player character and their treacherous friend, Eric Sparrow, on their quest to become professional skateboarders. The game was created with a theme of individuality: it stars an amateur skater in a true story mode, whereas each previous _Tony Hawk's_ game had starred professional skaters and had lacked a plot.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-handson-40) One reason for only allowing the player to use a custom character was that certain criminal acts completed in the plot would not reflect well on real-world skaters.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-egm_feature-41) Previous games in the series had included character-creation features as well, but Neversoft heavily expanded customization in _Underground_ by implementing face-scanning for the PlayStation 2 version.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-handson-40)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-ign-42) Regarding the customization options, especially the park editor, producer Stacey Drellishak stated that Neversoft was "trying to create the most customizable game ever".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-egm_feature-41) Levels in the console versions of _Underground_ were significantly larger than those of earlier _Tony Hawk's_ games. Neversoft expanded each level until it ceased to run correctly, then shrunk it slightly.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-ign-42) Most of the levels were modeled closely after real-world locations; the designers traveled to locales representative of each city in the game and took photographs and videos as reference.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-notes-43) Neversoft wanted the player to become familiar with the basic game mechanics quickly and to notice _Underground_'s differences from previous _Tony Hawk's_ games, who all stuck to roughly the same pattern, immediately. To accomplish this, they introduced the player to foot travel and the ability to climb along ledges in the first few missions of the game.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-thugged-44) While Neversoft wanted to keep _Underground_ realistic and relatable for the most part, they added driving missions as an enjoyable diversion and to push the boundaries of freedom in skateboarding games,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-notes-43) but these missions were intended not to take away from the main experience of skateboarding.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-thugged-44) Because _Pro Skater 4_ had received criticism for its difficulty, Neversoft added four difficulty settings to _Underground_'s story mode.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-45)

_[Tony Hawk's Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2 "Tony Hawk's Underground 2")_, released a year after its predecessor, was the only direct sequel in the series. While it still featured a story mode, it took a stark departure from _Underground_ and focused on a "World Destruction Tour" orchestrated by Tony Hawk and [Bam Margera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bam_Margera "Bam Margera"). As such, the game tried to capitalize on the immense popularity of _[Jackass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackass_/(franchise/) "Jackass (franchise)")_ and its related media by also focusing on destruction and self-deprecating pranks.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-IGN_Jackass-46) One later review referred to the game being "more of a _Jackass_ game than the [_Jackass_ game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackass:_The_Game "Jackass: The Game")".[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Jackass-47) This was reflected by the _Jackass_ stars [Jason "Wee-Man" Acuña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_%22Wee-Man%22_Acu%C3%B1a "Jason \"Wee-Man\" Acuña"), [Stephen "Steve-O" Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve-O "Steve-O"), Margera and his father [Phil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Margera "Phil Margera") featuring heavily in the game. Due to some fans being displeased with the absence of the goal-oriented approach of the _Pro Skater_ era, a "Classic Mode" showcasing the old gameplay was included from this entry onwards.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-IGN_Jackass-46) The [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable") exclusive _[Tony Hawk's Underground 2: Remix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2:_Remix "Tony Hawk's Underground 2: Remix")_ contained different levels and a slightly different story and was released in the spring of 2005. Former developer Chris Rausch recalled that at the time of _Underground_ and _Underground 2_, the control scheme of the series had reached its limit and Activision instructed Neversoft to develop each new entry around one single new gimmick, such as a story mode or vehicle controls in the _Underground_ subseries, or the [open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") of _[American Wasteland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_American_Wasteland "Tony Hawk's American Wasteland")_.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GameBrain_Interview-31)

In 2005, _American Wasteland_ was released on the PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube, Xbox 360 (as a launch title) and later on PC. The game's story mode is set in the city of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where the player character is trying to renovate a run-down [skatepark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skatepark "Skatepark"). While the game was advertised with featuring one huge comprehensive open world in story mode, the game's world was actually composed of several levels, resembling different [areas of Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_districts_and_neighborhoods_of_Los_Angeles "List of districts and neighborhoods of Los Angeles"), which were connected through [loading tunnels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loading_screen "Loading screen") to make them appear consecutive.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-48) Similar to _Underground 2_, the game includes a classic mode separate from the story mode, which mostly recycles levels of the PSP-exclusive _Underground 2: Remix_, released earlier that year. Furthermore, the game implemented [BMX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMX "BMX") controls similar to the _[Mat Hoffman's Pro BMX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat_Hoffman%27s_Pro_BMX "Mat Hoffman's Pro BMX")_ games, which were also released by Activision. Also similar to its predecessor, the game was accompanied by _[American Sk8land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_American_Sk8land "Tony Hawk's American Sk8land")_, a [handheld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_game_console "Handheld game console") game for [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") and [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") consoles with slightly different story and levels.

The promise of an open world skateboarding game was fulfilled with the next entry in the series, _[Project 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Project_8 "Tony Hawk's Project 8")_, released in late 2006. While the PS2 and Xbox versions did not feature said open world, the [seventh generation of video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Seventh generation of video game consoles"), such as the [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") and [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") could support larger content. Once again, the game's story centered on the player character aspiring to become a professional skateboarder, this time by advancing through a rank system to become a part of Tony Hawk's new fictional skateboarding team, the namegiving "Project 8". Unlike in previous entries, the classic mode was embedded in the different areas of the open world. The game did not appear on Nintendo's then-new [Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii "Wii") console, which instead saw the release of the then-exclusive [spin-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin-off_/(media/) "Spin-off (media)") game _[Downhill Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Downhill_Jam "Tony Hawk's Downhill Jam")_, a [downhill racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skateboarding_styles#Downhill_skateboarding "Skateboarding styles") game featuring a mostly fictitious cast. The game was also released on PS2 half a year later.

The next game in the main series, 2007's _[Proving Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Proving_Ground "Tony Hawk's Proving Ground")_ featured a largely similar concept to _Project 8_, with an open world and the player able to choose three career paths as a skater. [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), were established as the three open world areas, with each containing three skateable areas, which also featured an integrated classic mode. The game was the first and only entry of the series to compete with rival skateboarding series _[Skate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skate_/(2007_video_game/) "Skate (2007 video game)")_, which also featured an open world but with more advanced controls and a less arcade-style approach. _Skate_ outsold _Proving Ground_ on a 2:1 ratio, resembling its lackluster reception.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto2-49) With the franchise suffering from product fatigue and appearing to be past its prime, Activision decided to dedicate most of Neversoft's laborforce to the _[Guitar Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_Hero "Guitar Hero")_ and _[Call of Duty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_of_Duty "Call of Duty")_ franchises.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Infinity_Ward-51) This development would more and more marginalize Neversoft, which was defunct and completely merged with [Infinity Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity_Ward "Infinity Ward") by 2014.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Neversoft_Infinity_Ward-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-52) The control of the _Tony Hawk's_ franchise had passed on to [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") studio Robomodo by 2008.

### Robomodo era (2008–2015)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Hawk%27s&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Robomodo era (2008–2015)")\]

To combat product fatigue and be able to compete with rival [EA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA "EA")'s _Skate_ series, Activision decided to reboot the series with the new developer Robomodo.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Ride_Destructoid-53)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Ride_IGN-54) Due to this, no new entry in the main series was released in 2008, but the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") exclusive spin-off _[Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Motion "Tony Hawk's Motion")_ already hinted at the new franchise's new direction, as it featured tilt and motion controls.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-55) Furthermore, the game featured the option to [snowboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowboarding "Snowboarding") for the first time in the series' history.

In 2009, Robomodo released their first entry in the series, _[Tony Hawk: Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Ride "Tony Hawk: Ride")_, which relied on a [peripheral-supported controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peripheral "Peripheral") shaped like a skateboard. The game did not rely on a plot or an open world any longer and featured a completely different control system, with the player [railing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_%27em_up#rail_shooter "Shoot 'em up") down a predetermined route, trying to use the skateboard controller to perform tricks on predetermined obstacles. Activision promoted the game as the next step in the evolution of skateboarding video games, but the game sold poorly and critical reception was negative, with most critics calling the game's $120 price outrageous and the controls non-functioning.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Ride_Destructoid-53)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Ride_IGN-54) [GameTrailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameTrailers "GameTrailers") named it "Most Disappointing Game of 2009",[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto-7) while [GamesRadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesRadar "GamesRadar") named it "Worst Game of the Year".[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-56) Despite the game's poor reception, a sequel called _[Shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Shred "Tony Hawk: Shred")_ was released a year later. The game used the same mechanics and concept as its predecessor and reintroduced snowboarding, while aiming at a younger audience.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-57) Just like its predecessor, the game was a critical and commercial failure, selling merely 3000 copies in its first week of release in the US.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-58)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-59) A former developer of Neversoft stated that the idea of a peripheral-supported game came from Activision itself, who were eager to develop peripheral devices for every one of their franchises following the success of _Guitar Hero_.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GameBrain_Interview-31) In a 2012 interview, Hawk defended the idea of peripheral-supported games, stating that the original series had become "diluted" and unable to compete with _Skate_, which made developing games with the then-popular peripheral devices necessary. Furthermore, he blamed biased critics and rushed development for the commercial failure of the games.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-60)

Because all games in the series released since _American Wasteland_ failed to achieve commercial success, Activision decided to put the franchise on hold. When Robomodo was tasked with developing a new game, it was decided to return to the franchise's roots and develop a port of the original _Pro Skater_ series. _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater HD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_HD "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater HD")_ was released in the summer of 2012 via [download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Download "Download") only and featured a collection of popular levels from _Pro Skater 1–3_. Critical reception towards the game was mixed, as while critics felt that it captured the appeal of the original games, the content was described as sparse, while the game was said to not deliver updated gameplay mechanics and feel dated.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-dtoid_review-61)[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-62) In 2014, the endless runner _[Shred Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Shred_Session "Tony Hawk's Shred Session")_ [soft launched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_launch "Soft launch") for [mobile devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_device "Mobile device") in a handful of territories but was later pulled from the market, postponed indefinitely and later shelved.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-63)

After having only produced spin-offs and ports since inheriting the franchise in 2008, Activision announced in mid-2015 a traditional entry in the series developed by Robomodo for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, [PlayStation 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_4 "PlayStation 4"), and [Xbox One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_One "Xbox One"). To point out its return to the series' roots and heyday, it was named _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_5 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5")_. According to Hawk, Robomodo consulted with some former [Neversoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neversoft "Neversoft") employees to ensure that the gameplay felt like the original _Pro Skater_ games.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-64) Because the [licensing deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/License "License") between Activision and Tony Hawk was set to expire by the end of 2015, the game was hastily developed within a few months and released unfinished with little promotion.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-65)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-66) After initial footage received negative feedback by fans and commentators alike for its completely outdated graphics, Robomodo made a complete departure from the attempted realistic look to a [cel-shaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cel_shading "Cel shading") style two months prior to the game's release. Even though Activision marketed this as a conscious stylistic decision unrelated to the feedback and solely owing to allow a consistent [frame rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_rate "Frame rate"),[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-67)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-68) the end results did not save the game from being [panned by critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_notable_for_negative_reception "List of video games notable for negative reception") upon release in September 2015. Most critics noted that the graphics were inferior even to the games released on the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"), while the gameplay barely resembled previous releases and the fact that the game was rendered almost unplayable by numerous [bugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug "Software bug"). Furthermore, the simplistic, bland environments and missions, as well as the complete absence of [NPCs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character "Non-player character") were noted, while some critics pointed out that better levels could have been designed with the Create-a-Park feature of previous games, whereas most levels were simply inferior copies of levels from the original games.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Broken-69)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto3-70)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto4-71) The game was so rushed to release that it was unplayable without an 8GB [day one patch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patch_/(computing/) "Patch (computing)"), with only the [tutorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutorial "Tutorial") and park creator being accessible.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Broken-69)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto5-72) _Pro Skater 5_ has the fourth-lowest average score of any PlayStation 4 game[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto6-73) and the fifth-lowest average score of any Xbox One game[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto7-74) and was named the "Worst Video Game of 2015" by _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto1-8) _[Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_/(magazine/) "Edge (magazine)")_ described it as "an insult to its history, to its licensed skaters and sponsors, to modern hardware, and to anyone who plays it".[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto8-75) By the end of the year, the license had run out and was not renewed. Robomodo went out of business soon thereafter for unknown reasons.

### Hiatus and return (2016–present)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Hawk%27s&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Hiatus and return (2016–present)")\]

The initial licensing deal between Hawk and Activision expired in December 2015.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-VR/Expired-1) In January 2017, Hawk said in an interview that he was in early talks to continue the franchise without Activision[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-76)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-77) and that he was interested in using [virtual reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_reality "Virtual reality") for his next game.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-VR/Expired-1) That November, Hawk stated that while he would agree to support the future installments under the _Pro Skater_ moniker, Activision owned all rights to the license and thus controlled whether future games would be made.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Wired-9) Meanwhile, fans of Neversoft's original series continued to preserve its levels through _[THUG Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THUG_Pro "THUG Pro")_, an [online multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_multiplayer "Online multiplayer") [fangame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fangame "Fangame") made using _[Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2 "Tony Hawk's Underground 2")'_s engine.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-hester1-10)

The first game bearing his name and not to be published by Activision, _[Tony Hawk's Skate Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Skate_Jam "Tony Hawk's Skate Jam")_, was released for [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS") and [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_/(operating_system/) "Android (operating system)") in December 2018.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-toucharcade.com-11)

In 2020, [Vicarious Visions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicarious_Visions "Vicarious Visions") remastered the first two _Pro Skater_ games for Microsoft Windows, [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch"), PlayStation 4, [PlayStation 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_5 "PlayStation 5"), [Xbox Series X/S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Series_X/S "Xbox Series X/S") and Xbox One as _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_1_%2B_2 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2")_. It was released on September 4, once again published by Activision. All levels and skaters from the original games returned in the remaster, and improvements to the skater and park creation tools were added to allow these to be shared online in multiplayer modes. In addition to new songs, the majority of the music from the original games returned as well, with a few exceptions due to licensing issues.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-engadget_remastered_1+2-78)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-79) Hawk claimed that remasters of _Pro Skater 3_ and _4_ were planned for development following the release of _1 + 2_, but these were cancelled due to Vicarious Visions being merged with Blizzard.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-80)

On February 18, 2025, skateboarder [Tyshawn Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyshawn_Jones "Tyshawn Jones"), who appeared in _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2_, claimed that new _Pro Skater_ remasters were in development and that he was involved.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-81) On February 20, a teaser for an upcoming game was unveiled in a multiplayer map for _[Call of Duty: Black Ops 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_of_Duty:_Black_Ops_6 "Call of Duty: Black Ops 6")_. The teaser, depicting the date 03.04.25, was speculated to be in reference to _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3_ and _4_.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Deschamps-82) On February 25, _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 + 4_ was rated by Singapore ratings board Infocomm Media Development Authority for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-83) On March 4, _[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 + 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_3_%2B_4 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 + 4")_ was officially confirmed with a reveal trailer and a release date set for July 11, 2025. Also announced was a digital deluxe edition featuring bonus skaters, soundtrack songs, new decks, clothing for create-a-skater and special version of Tony Hawk.

_Tony Hawk's Pro Skater_ was critically acclaimed. [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN") gave the N64 version of the game a 9.1 out of 10 praising the gameplay for "genius control, combo system and design" despite little criticism with sound stating "the punk tracks are dumbed down and looped".[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-221) It also gave the PlayStation version an outstanding rating (9.4 out of 10) again praising the gameplay and the graphics stating it is "simple but amazing in terms of animations, physics, and size of levels".[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-222) _Pro Skater 2_ was met with critical acclaim and commercial success, greatly surpassing its [predecessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater"). According to [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), it holds a score of 98/100, making it one of the highest rated video games of all time across all consoles and platforms. _Pro Skater 2_ along with _[Soulcalibur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soulcalibur_/(video_game/) "Soulcalibur (video game)")_, and _[Grand Theft Auto IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_IV "Grand Theft Auto IV")_ are ranked second behind _[The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legend_of_Zelda:_Ocarina_of_Time "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time")_.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-MC-3)[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Highest-223) [Jeff Gerstmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Gerstmann "Jeff Gerstmann") of [GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot") praised the PlayStation version, awarding it 9.9/10, saying "as most major publishers' development efforts shift to any number of next-generation platforms, _Tony Hawk 2_ will likely stand as one of the last truly fantastic games to be released on the PlayStation".[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-224) The PlayStation version of the game received a score of 10 out of 10 from the magazine _[Game Informer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Informer "Game Informer")_, while the rest of the other versions for other consoles received lower scores. In Japan, _[Famitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famitsu "Famitsu")_ magazine scored the Game Boy Advance version of the game a 33 out of 40[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-225) and the PlayStation version of the game a 28 out of 40.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-226) In the final issue of the [Official UK PlayStation Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_UK_PlayStation_Magazine "Official UK PlayStation Magazine"), the game was chosen as the 7th best game of all time.[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-227) _[Game Informer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Informer "Game Informer")_ named it the fourth best game ever made in 2001. The staff praised the game for its growth over its predecessor and its impact on its genre.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-228) Similarly, the PS2 version of _Pro Skater 3_ earned a rare perfect 10 score from [GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot"), one of only eleven games to ever receive said score.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-229)[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-230) It was also awarded the best sports game award at [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Entertainment_Expo "Electronic Entertainment Expo") 2001. [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN") rated the game 9.7/10, stating that the game "should go down in history as one of the best twitch-fests on PS2".[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-231) The game is currently the top rated PS2 game on the review aggregate website [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), with an average score of 97/100, tying with _[Grand Theft Auto III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_III "Grand Theft Auto III")_.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PS2-5) Famitsu gave the game a 30/40.[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-232) As for _Pro Skater 4_, IGN gave the Xbox version a 9/10, stating that "_Tony Hawk 4_ is by far the best skateboarding title around and head and shoulders above its 'me-too' competition".[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-233) The PlayStation 2 version received the highest score from IGN, with a 9.3/10, commenting that though the graphics haven't changed from its predecessor, the maps are much larger than in _Pro Skater 3_, along with praising the increased difficulty.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-234)

_Underground_ was released to critical acclaim: with scores for the PlayStation 2 at 90/100 on [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic").[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-MCPS2-132) GameZone's Michael Knutson stated that _Underground_ is "one of the best skating games around" and that players of every skill level would enjoy it.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamezone-235) [Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")'s Tom Bramwell concurred that "as a 'pick-up-and-play' sort of game, _THUG_ is endlessly rewarding" and called it the best entry in series.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-euro-236) The story was especially well received. Joe Rybicki of _[Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_U.S._PlayStation_Magazine "Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine")_ said that the title, as an extreme-sports game, has a real story with "honest-to-goodness characters".[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-opm-237) [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")'s Douglas Perry called it "a kick, albeit relatively lightweight in nature". He especially praised the pervasive sense of humor in the narrative and in the portrayal of real-world skaters.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-ign_2-238) Knutson called the story "unique" and said that it blends well with the gameplay.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamezone-235) The alternate gameplay modes were received very well. Knutson lauded the game's high degree of customization; he summarized that "everything is expounded a hundred fold: from create-a-skater to create-a-park mode, it is simply amazing". He singled out the level editor as one of the deepest he had ever seen.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamezone-235) [GameSpy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpy "GameSpy")'s Bryn Williams identified the level editor as an "extremely well-designed" feature that contributed to the overall "brilliance" of the full product.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamespy-239) Leeper said that each customization mode is "intuitive and user-friendly", and both he and Rybicki especially enjoyed the trick-creation feature.[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gi-240)[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-opm-237) Reviewers for _[Famitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famitsu "Famitsu")_ magazine praised the story mode, whose [open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") format they compared to the _[Grand Theft Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto "Grand Theft Auto")_ series.[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-famitsu-241) Knutson and Perry enjoyed the multiplayer, particularly the online Firefight mode.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamezone-235) Williams thought similarly and stated that "the most notable disappointment" of the game was the lack of online play for non-PlayStation 2 owners.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamespy-239) Harris found the board customization of the Game Boy Advance version to be poorly implemented, though in-depth.[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-ign_gba-242) Despite his praise for the customization modes, Leeper admitted that his greatest enjoyment still came from "seeking out great lines and beating my scores".[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gi-240) While it still got fairly high reviews, critics criticized the story of _Underground 2_ and some critics noted that the gameplay had not been significantly upgraded from _Underground_. Silverman and Perry were unimpressed with the short selection of moves introduced in _Underground 2_.[\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-243) GameSpot agreed, but concluded that "while not all of these changes are all that great, the core gameplay in _THUG2_ is still very strong".[\[244\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-244) In contrast, Bramwell felt that the Sticker Slap and additional flip and grab tricks were meaningful, enjoyable additions.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-245) The addition of Classic mode, was praised by [1UP.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1UP.com "1UP.com"), who considered it superior to the Story mode in terms of levels, while adding that "gamers weaned on PS1 Hawks will shed a tear, while newer fans will get a lesson on how things started".[\[246\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-1UPXbox-246) _American Wasteland's_ reception was largely similar to that of _Underground 2_, with the exception that most critics were fond of the game's story. Chris Roper of [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN") praised Neversoft's decision to "go back to its roots and make a game about skating" as opposed to "the chaos and destruction of the _Underground_ games". Jeff Gerstmann of [GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot") stated that the saving grace of the game is a story mode that follows a 'ragtag group of misfits' who struggle to save the place they call home from evil real estate moguls' plot, and that "along the way, the characters become a little endearing". Reviews for Neversoft's entries started to dip with the release of _Project 8_. In the [GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot") review of the PlayStation 3 version, _Project 8_ was criticized for its lack of online play on Sony systems and unstable [frame rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_rate "Frame rate"), with critics noting that the series was becoming more and more stale.[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-247) _Proving Ground_ was met with mixed to positive reviews upon release. On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), both the [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") and [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") versions had an average score of 73/100 and 72/100,[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PGPS3-185)[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PGX360-186) the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2") version had an average score of 65/100,[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PGPS2-187) and the [Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii "Wii") version had an average score of 57/100.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PGWII-188) All of these scores are considered "mixed or average" by the site. The PlayStation 2 and Nintendo Wii versions were criticized for not having the same mechanics that are in the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions. The [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") version received generally favorable reviews from critics. On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") it received an average score of 79/100 based on 21 reviews.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-PGNDS-184)

As Robomodo began producing _Tony Hawk's_ games, the reviews immediately dropped deep into negative. _Tony Hawk: Ride_ received negative reviews from critics. The Metacritic average score of 47/100,[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-RWII-194) 46/100,[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-RX360-195) and 44/100[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-RPS3-196) for the PlayStation 3, Wii, and Xbox 360 versions respectively indicates "generally unfavorable reviews". [GameTrailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameTrailers "GameTrailers") gave _Tony Hawk: Ride_ a score 4.6[\[248\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-248) and named it Most Disappointing Game of 2009,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto-7) while [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN") gave the game a 5.0.[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-249) Both G4TV[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-250) and Giant Bomb[\[251\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-251) rated it 1/5. GameSpot gave it a 3.5/10,[\[252\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-252) with the only positive emblem the game received being that the peripheral was "sturdy". [GamesRadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesRadar "GamesRadar") gave the game 4/10.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-253) They also named it the worst game of the year, using its skateboard peripheral as the trophy for the "Anti-Awards" feature.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamesradar.com-6) _[Game Informer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Informer "Game Informer")_ gave it a 5.75, remarking that "as a skateboarder and as a gamer, _Tony Hawk: Ride_ is a curious idea but a letdown in practice. The huge level of frustration is not worth the time it takes to master the awkward gameplay idiosyncrasies".[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-254) Unlike its predecessors, _Pro Skater HD_ was able to at least attain mixed reviews. [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")'s Nic Vargas gave the game a score of 8/10, praising its purist gameplay whilst lamenting the lack of certain modes such as park creator and split screen multiplayer.[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-ign_review-255) The reviewer from [GameTrailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameTrailers "GameTrailers") gave the game a score of 7.4 and wrote that _Pro Skater HD_ "isn't flawless, but... it at least gets off on the right foot".[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gt_review-256) Lucas Sullivan of [GamesRadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesRadar "GamesRadar") felt that old-school fans of the franchise will be disappointed by what the game lacks, and gamers who never player the original games on PS1 will find the mechanics and level design sparse.[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gradar_review-257) [Destructoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destructoid "Destructoid") gave the game 4.5/10, stating that the execution isn't handled as well as the original games, as well as some of the design choices the developer made.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-dtoid_review-61) [G4TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G4_/(American_TV_channel/) "G4 (American TV channel)") gave the game a 4.5/5 and praised the console versions' online multiplayer and soundtrack.[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-G4_review-258) _[Official Xbox Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Xbox_Magazine "Official Xbox Magazine")_ gave _Pro Skater HD_ an 8/10. They praised the game's new big head mode.[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-oxm_review-259) _Pro Skater 5_ reverted to catastrophic reviews again and was [bashed by critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_notable_for_negative_reception "List of video games notable for negative reception") upon release in September 2015. Most critics noted that the graphics were inferior even to the games released on the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"), while the gameplay barely resembled previous releases and was rendered almost unplayable by numerous [bugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug "Software bug"). Furthermore, the simplistic, bland environments and missions and complete absence of [NPCs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character "Non-player character") were noted, and some critics pointed out that better levels could have been designed with the Create-a-Park feature of previous games, while most levels were simply inferior copies of levels from the original games.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Broken-69)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto3-70)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto4-71) The game was so rushed to release that it was unplayable without an 8GB [day one patch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patch_/(computing/) "Patch (computing)"), with only the [tutorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutorial "Tutorial") and park creator being accessible.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-Broken-69)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto5-72) _Pro Skater 5_ has the fourth-lowest average score of any PlayStation 4 game[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto6-73) and the fifth-lowest average score of any Xbox One game[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto7-74) and was named the "Worst Video Game of 2015" by _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto1-8) _[Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_/(magazine/) "Edge (magazine)")_ even went so far to call _Pro Skater 5_ "an insult to its history, to its licensed skaters and sponsors, to modern hardware, and to anyone who plays it".[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto8-75)

### Commercial reception

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Hawk%27s&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Commercial reception")\]

The PlayStation version of _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater_ received a "Platinum" sales award from the [Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_and_Leisure_Software_Publishers_Association "Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association") (ELSPA),[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-platinumelspa-260) indicating sales of at least 300,000 copies in the United Kingdom.[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamasutrasales-261) In the United States, _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2_'s computer version sold 320,000 copies and earned $8.0 million by August 2006, after its release in October 2000. It was the country's 58th best-selling computer game between January 2000 and August 2006. Combined sales of all _Pro Skater_ computer games released between January 2000 and August 2006 had reached 440,000 units in the United States by the latter date.[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-edgesales-262) Also in the United States, the game's [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") version sold 680,000 copies and earned $24 million by August 2006. During the period between January 2000 and August 2006, it was the 38th highest-selling game launched for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"), [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") or [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable") in that country.[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-nextgensales-263) The game's PlayStation version received a "Platinum" sales award from the ELSPA.[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamasutrasales-261) By July 2006, the PlayStation 2 version of _Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3_ had sold 2.1 million copies and earned $77 million in the United States. _[Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Generation_/(magazine/) "Next Generation (magazine)")_ ranked it as the 14th highest-selling game launched for the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"), [Xbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_/(console/) "Xbox (console)") or [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country. Combined sales of _Tony Hawk_ console games released in the 2000s reached 10.7 million units in the United States by July 2006.[\[264\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-nextgensales2-264) Its PlayStation 2 version also received a "Platinum" sales award from the ELSPA.[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamasutrasales-261)

In Europe, the PlayStation 2, Xbox, and GameCube versions of _Underground_ were respectively the fifth, sixth, and eighth-best selling games for those consoles the week after the game's release.[\[265\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-265)[\[266\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-266)[\[267\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-267) It would remain uninterrupted in the top twenty of every week until January 24, 2004, for the Xbox and GameCube[\[268\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-268)[\[269\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-269) and February 21 for the PlayStation 2, inclusive.[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-270) As of December 2007, the PlayStation 2 edition of the game had sold 2.11 million copies in the United States.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-271) The GameCube version made Nintendo's [Player's Choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Selects "Nintendo Selects") list by selling 250,000 copies in the United States.[\[272\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-272) Its PlayStation 2 version also received a "Platinum" sales award from the ELSPA.[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-gamasutrasales-261) _Skate_ outsold _Proving Ground_ on a 2:1 ratio, resembling its lackluster reception.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-auto2-49)

In the first month of its U.S. release, _Tony Hawk: Ride_ sold 114,000 copies.[\[273\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-273) During its first week on sale in the United States, _[Tony Hawk: Shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk:_Shred "Tony Hawk: Shred")_ sold 3,000 copies.[\[274\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-274)[\[275\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-275) Due to this, former developer Chris Rausch described _Shred_ as the game that had killed the series and he expected no new game for release in the foreseeable future.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-GameBrain_Interview-31)

_[Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Pro_Skater_1_%2B_2 "Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2")_ became the fastest selling game in the franchise according to [Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision "Activision"), selling 1 million copies within the first two weeks.[\[276\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-276) In the United Kingdom the game was the biggest launch in the franchise since _Underground_.[\[277\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-277)

The brand brought in about $715 million in revenue by 2004.[\[278\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-278)

During a period of series inactivity caused by the lapse of Activision's contract with Hawk, the _Tony Hawk's_ fanbase largely sustained itself through _[THUG Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THUG_Pro "THUG Pro")_, a fan-made [total conversion mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_conversion "Total conversion") of _[Tony Hawk's Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s_Underground_2 "Tony Hawk's Underground 2")_ for [Microsoft Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") that features levels of every game in the series for use in online multiplayer.[\[279\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-279)

A documentary about the _Pro Skater_ series was developed by former [Neversoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neversoft "Neversoft") employee and producer of the series, Ralph D'Amato. The documentary, _Pretending I'm a Superman: The Tony Hawk Video Game Story_, features interviews from former Neversoft employees as well as skaters featured throughout the series, including Hawk himself and is directed by Ludvig Gür.[\[280\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-280) The documentary came about after D'Amato had taken Gür, who was visiting him in California in 2016, to meet Hawk briefly but which turned out to be several hours discussing the possibility of documentary, which was further developed after more online calls and emails. The documentary's name is based on the song "Superman" by the band [Goldfinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldfinger_/(band/) "Goldfinger (band)") which was featured on the first game's soundtrack.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-281) The film was released on August 18, 2020.[\[282\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Hawk%27s#cite_note-282)

Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 2, Game Boy Advance
==========================================

[January 19, 2022](https://thekingofgrabs.com/2022/01/19/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2-game-boy-advance/) [Mallo](https://thekingofgrabs.com/author/thekingofgrabs/) [Leave a comment](https://thekingofgrabs.com/2022/01/19/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2-game-boy-advance/#respond)

Developed by **_Vicarious Visions_** and published by **_Activision_** in **_2001_**, **_Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 2_** on the **_Game Boy Advance_** is one of those games that you’d expect not to work that well – being a handheld conversion of a popular and successful 3D game – but it actually turns out to be a fantastic game in its own right.

Instead of [the _**PlayStation**_ original](https://thekingofgrabs.com/2018/01/07/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2-playstation/)‘s third-person viewpoint the developers have chosen an isometric view for the _**GBA**_ port and it works very well. All the courses and challenges are recognisable, and it’s just as much fun skateboarding in this as it was in the original.

Of course there’s a slight downside, and that is that the famous soundtrack has been (necessarily) truncated into shortened instrumental versions of the music that was featured in the original game. That was unavoidable, though, since the original soundtrack was Red Book audio streaming directly off the CD-ROM that it came on. For a handheld cartridge version they were obviously not able to do that. But it’s a small price to pay and _**Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 2**_ on the **_Game Boy Advance_** remains a great game. Arguably one of the best on the system.

See also: [THPS2](https://thekingofgrabs.com/2018/01/07/tony-hawks-pro-skater-2-playstation/), [THPS3](https://thekingofgrabs.com/2018/01/07/tony-hawks-pro-skater-3-playstation/), and [THPS4](https://thekingofgrabs.com/2018/01/07/tony-hawks-pro-skater-4-playstation/).

### Summary

Pull off a 50 or 50 grind, throw up a hand-plant, catch massive air, and stick a few ollies in this hand-held gem. You'll get your choice of 13 of the world's best skaters (including Tony Hawk, of course), as you move from street to park in this detailed update on the popular PRO SKATER series. No more incidents with the cops, skinned knees, stupid-looking helmets, or run-ins with street punks; this game brings you all of the action of real skating without any of the hang-ups. Cool graphics, a killer soundtrack, and epic gameplay make TONY HAWK'S PRO-SKATER 2 a must-have.

34.content:
Folks, if you haven't been excited about the Game Boy Advance system yet ¿ you have a reason to get excited now.A few days ago, [Activision](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025004.html) gave us a quick glimpse of _Tony Hawk Pro Skater 2_ with a single screenshot. Today at Nintendo's press event at Camp Game Boy Advance, the game was completely playable. Super Mario Advance and F-Zero, you've both got serious competition when this game hits the shelves on launch day.

The game is being developed by [Vicarious Visions](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025232.html), the same development company responsible for _Spider-Man_ and _Polaris Sno-Cross_ for the Game Boy Color. The team has really done their homework on what makes Tony Hawk work on the console versions, as the GBA edition is absolutely stunning, both in looks and in playability.

What the development team has done is take high-resolution models of the track layouts in the console versions, and fix them in an overhead angled perspective. For the skaters, the developers have constructed them into 300 polygon models with no textures ¿ at the size of the guy on-screen, you'd never notice the lack of facial or clothing detail on these guys. The overall effect is absolutely amazing, as the game runs at a constant 60 frames per second with zero drop in the action. The game design is exactly the same as the console editions, right down to the physics of the skater ¿ he flows across the floor and soars through the air with the same grace as the 3D versions of the title. The game even simulates the bloodspray that's left on the ground when the skater spills off a jump.

So far I've only been able to play the Hangar level, as the early version lacked a battery save to record all the quotas being scored throughout the play session (and there _will_ be battery save when the game's ready to ship). And though I'm not an absolute expert in Tony Hawk, I've put in quite a few hours on the Dreamcast edition ¿ and the Game Boy Advance version looks and feels so much like that game it's downright scary. All the elements are in place ¿ grinding the helicopter blades, knocking over the barrels, grabbing S, K, A, T, and E...if you did it in the console version, you're going to do it here.

There are drawbacks to fixing the perspective at an isometric, overhead angle, though, and the developers had a lot of design issues to work out to make it work. The most concerning issue is the fact that it's super hard to judge angles and objects at different levels ¿ hovering money looks like it's ground-based, so you'll have to look at the shadows they're leaving on the floor to understand just where they're located. Your skater will also go behind objects, but the programmers make the objects transparent so you can see what your on-screen persona's doing.

The controls also had to be sandwiched onto the Game Boy Advance button layout. The shoulder buttons are now kickflips and grinds instead of skater rotation ¿ there is a slight learning curve to playing _Tony Hawk_ on the GBA, but after 10 minutes I figured it all out. I starting pulling off four and five move combos just as gracefully as I can on the Dreamcast edition.

I'd tell you more, but I've got to get back to the action ¿ trust me when I say that you're going to want this game. Badly. Pre-order that Game Boy Advance...and a copy of _Tony Hawk_ while you're at it.

_\-- Craig Harris_
